description: This is a highly enthusiastic and innovative group of people who enjoy experimenting with novel ideas, solving difficult issues, and developing practical solutions. Critical thinking and learning are highly regarded by our team. What we need now are some energetic members with various competencies, unique viewpoints, and the drive to contribute positively. Those who wish to test boundaries, contribute ideas, and achieve something substantial may apply for membership to our team.
summary:
Season Simulator is an online tools that simulates a farm "flight simulator". It replay every real growing season from 1984 to today at any location, using daily weather data from NASA POWER. It compares your current rotation with alternatives on 4 factors: water for irrigation, heat during crops' most vulnerable weeks, soil health, and 1-year to the next reproducibility.

It solves the Field Shift problem by transforming generations of NASA data into one advice. And that advice comes with an explanation, a printable field card and transparent boundaries. Plus it recommends rotations appropriate for every site, and shows how NASA's seasonal forecast can change the road ahead.

That's important in areas such as Egypt's Nile delta, where water is limited and spring heat can seriously damage wheat. Farmers in that region require reliable information, in either English or Arabic, on all types of phones. The tool provides backup for the judgement of the farmer and local advisors, not a substitute.
details:
The farmer chooses a location on the map. The app displaysNASA POWER historic daily data for that location for more than 40 years: temperature, dew point, wind, solar radiation and rainfall.
Every day, it calculates crop water use based on the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith (our code is an exact reproduction of FAO's worked example). It then calculates the volume of irrigation water to be applied, based on FAO calculations of effective rainfall, irrigation efficiency, and flooded rice.
It runs through each season for all rotations. For each season it estimates the number of hot days during each crop's sensitive time (for example grain filling for wheat). It also estimates the number of days of bare soil, legumes and salt risk based on the farmer's personal soil test.
The farmer chooses priorities (water, heat, soil, feed). The app lines up the plans and describes the position of the best plan in a sentence. If two plans are close in ranking, it says so, rather than listing just one winner.

More features:

Plans proposed for each place, based on 234 pairs of crops (38 crops in total, including vegetables and fruit trees);

a sowing-date slider;

NASA's GEOS-S2S seasonal forecast: The season ahead;

a printable field card;

A beginner's helper chat that reads the results only from the app.

Benefits

"The farmers know what the water is worth in cubic metres of water per feddan. For instance at Shebin El-Kom it would mean 1 750 m³ of water less per feddan per annum to grow wheat-maize instead of wheat-rice."
The slider indicates that sowing wheat in early November instead of late December reduces hot grain-filling days from an average of approximately 14 to only approximately 2.5.
We tag each result as calculated, known crop trait or from the farmer's soil test and each result has its own confidence badge.

Intended impact

Assist extension staff and farmers in selecting the most water-efficient, damage-free crop rotations, based on past weather data from the farmer's local district.
Show me what I'm trading off. For instance, for soil improvement a legume can postpone the wheat sowing into warmer weather.
Work anywhere on the planet, not just in Egypt.

Tools and technology

Source: Data from: NASA POWER Daily API (AG community) and NASA GMAO GEOS-S2S seasonal forecasts.
Methods: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Papers 56 and 29, and FAO irrigation manuals.
Code: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript (ES modules) with no build step.
Libraries and services: Leaflet with Open Street Map as map Chart.js for the charts.
Testing and data scripts: Node.js.
Hosting: GitHub Pages.
The app does not show any output from the AI model.

Creativity

The flight-simulator concept: reliving actual, past seasons instead of speculating.
Crash-test stars are from the five worst seasons in each plan.
Coptic farming-calendar dates next to Gregorian dates.
A "memory check": Farmers can compare the year they remember as bad versus the years the app considers worst.
Brief one with visuals for occasional readers, detailed one for experts.

Factors we considered

Honesty:

For past temperatures, we adjust NASA's grid-cell data to our official weather-station normals.
We do not 'generate' a number; all values are from published sources.
Heat numbers are not indicators of yields, they are indicators of exposure.
No profit score for the app because it has no price data.
English and Arabic – The lay-out is right-to-left, it is light so it can be used with old phones, and it is available in a offline mode (used for the demo farm).
Respect for local knowledge: all cards conclude with questions to be asked of the farmer's agronomist.
